text: You designed a landing zone in Chapter 2 around management groups or an AWS Organization specifically so you could attach rules once, at the top, and have them apply everywhere beneath. Policy is the first thing that hierarchy is actually for. If you configure encryption requirements and tagging rules one subscription at a time by hand, you've thrown away the entire point of building that hierarchy in the first place.

In Azure, individual policy definitions get bundled into an initiative — a policy set like a platform baseline covering tagging, allowed regions, and encryption together. The part that makes this organization-wide is where you assign it: an assignment at a management group scope inherits down to every subscription nested underneath, including subscriptions that don't exist yet. A team vends a new subscription next quarter, and it lands under the right management group already subject to the baseline, with no one remembering to reattach anything.

Assignment effects matter. Deny blocks a non-compliant resource at creation. Audit lets it through but flags it as non-compliant in reporting. DeployIfNotExists can actively remediate, like attaching a missing diagnostic setting. Real baselines mix Deny for rules that must never be violated with Audit for rules that need visibility before anyone's comfortable blocking on them.

AWS splits this into two mechanisms that are easy to confuse. A Service Control Policy attaches to an Organizational Unit and sets a hard ceiling on allowed API actions for every identity underneath — even the account's own root user can't exceed it. AWS Config rules do something different: they continuously evaluate resources that already exist and report compliance, the AWS equivalent of Azure Policy's Audit effect. SCPs prevent; Config rules detect. A mature landing zone uses both.

The architectural point underneath all of it: policy definitions, initiative assignments, and SCPs are infrastructure, so they belong in the same Terraform pipeline from course 8 as everything else — not a separate manual process. That gets you something portal-managed policy never gives you: a pull request diff showing exactly what governance rule changed, who approved it, and when, which is exactly the evidence a review board or an auditor asks for directly.
